# How I want my resume written

The AI reads this guide each time it writes a resume. Change it to suit you.

## Who reads my resume

Two readers decide whether I get a call. Write for both.

- **Screening software.** The employer's system turns my file into plain text. AI tools then check it against each requirement in the ad, one at a time. If they can't find clear proof of a requirement, they treat it as missing. Recruiters also search the text for exact words, such as a job title or a tool.
- **A busy recruiter.** The first look takes a few seconds. They check my name, my last two job titles, employers and dates, and my education, plus the summary and skills at the top. If those match the ad, they read on.

## Facts come first

- Use only facts from my master profile. If you're not sure of something, leave it out. You can't ask me questions here.
- My master profile decides what's true and how to describe me. Follow its rules on job titles, years of experience, numbers and their labels, wording to avoid, roles to leave off, and the "Don't claim", "To confirm" and ⚠ items.
- This guide decides how to write the resume. My profile may have its own notes on layout, section order, date format, length or style. Where they differ from this guide, follow this guide.
- Skip any steps in my profile that don't fit here, such as asking me questions, making a Word file or updating the profile.
- The ad's own instructions (such as a page limit) beat this guide.

## Step 1: map the ad (in your thinking, before you write)

Read the full ad. The lists under "The job" come from an AI's reading of the ad, and they can miss things.

List these, one short line each:

- every must-have, including qualifications and work rights;
- every "desirable" or "nice to have" item;
- the main duties;
- the ad's key words (the job title, tools, methods and domain words), spelt exactly as the ad spells them.

For each item, note the best proof in my profile (which role, which fact). Mark it **strong**, **partial** or **none**.

Then decide:

- which two or three proofs lead (they go in the summary and the top bullets);
- which roles get full detail, which get one line, and which get dropped.

## Step 2: write it

### Order and headings

Use these headings, in this order. Screening software looks for standard names.

1. `# [My name]`, then one line with my contact details.
2. `## Summary`
3. `## Skills`
4. `## Certifications` goes here if the ad asks for a certification I hold, or if mine are central to the role.
5. `## Experience`
6. `## Projects`, only if my profile has one that supports this ad and doesn't already list it under Experience.
7. `## Certifications` goes here in all other cases. Leave it out if I have none.
8. `## Education`
9. A last line: "Referees available on request." If the ad asks for referees, still write only this line. My profile doesn't hold their details.

### Contact line

- Suburb, state and postcode, then email, phone, and LinkedIn if my profile has it, separated by " | ".
- Add work rights, citizenship or a security clearance only if my profile states it.
- No street address, photo, date of birth, age, gender, marital status, nationality or religion.

### Summary

- Three or four lines (about 50 to 70 words). No "I", "me" or "my".
- Start with what I am, in the ad's words where they're true of me, plus my years of experience. Never change a real job title to match the ad.
- Then give my two or three strongest proofs for this ad. Use one number if my profile has one.
- It's not an objective: say what I offer, not what I want.

### Skills

- Three to six rows, each a bullet with a bold label, for example `- **Frontend:** React, TypeScript, …`.
- Put the most relevant row first, and the ad's terms first in each row.
- About eight items per row at most. List only skills my profile backs up.
- Add a "Ways of working" row when the ad asks for things like Agile, code review or mentoring.
- Leave out old or basic tools the ad doesn't ask for.

### Experience

- Newest first. Each role starts with a heading in one fixed format: `### [Job title] | [Employer] | [Mon YYYY] – [Mon YYYY]`. Use "present" for a current role.
- Give the month and year for every role, for example "Aug 2024 – Jun 2025". Recruiters and screening software work out my years of experience from these dates. Use years alone only when my profile gives no month, and never guess a month.
- You may add one short line under the heading for context, such as what the employer does or the scale.
- For several client projects at one consultancy, use one heading for the consultancy and its dates. Then give each client role a bold line, `**[Job title], [Client] | [Mon YYYY] – [Mon YYYY]**`, with its bullets. This shows one long stay, not many short jobs.
- Older or less relevant roles go at the end under `### Earlier experience`, one line each: `- **[Job title], [Employer]** ([Mon YYYY] – [Mon YYYY]): [what I did that matters here].`

How much each role gets:

- Recent roles that match this ad: four to six bullets.
- Other roles from the last 10 to 15 years: two or three bullets.
- Older roles: one line, or nothing. Keep the one line if it shows a must-have (such as a language the ad asks for) or backs up my years of experience.
- If my dates leave a gap of six months or more, and my profile says why, add one honest line. If it doesn't say why, leave the gap.

### Bullets

- One idea each. One line is best, two at most.
- Start with a verb: past tense for past roles, present tense for my current role. Vary the verbs.
- Put the words that matter first. Readers often see only the first two or three.
- Shape: what I did, how I did it (the tool or method, in the ad's words), and what changed. Lead with the result when it's the strongest part.
- Use numbers only from my profile, with their labels ("about", "roughly", "estimate"). Never round up.
- No result on record? Show the scale instead: team size, users, systems, sites or regions.
- Made-up example of the shape (never copy its facts):
  - Weak: "Responsible for the booking system's frontend."
  - Strong: "Rebuilt the booking frontend in React and TypeScript, cutting page load from 6 to 2 seconds."

### Keywords

- For each must-have that I can prove, use the ad's exact words at least once in a bullet that shows me doing it. If it's a skill, put it in Skills too. A Skills list on its own isn't enough: some systems don't read it.
- Each nice-to-have I can prove should appear at least once. Skills is enough.
- Write the ad's spelling of tools ("Node.js", not "NodeJS", if that's how the ad has it).
- Give the full form and the short form of a key acronym once, for example "Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG)". Use the short form after that.
- Once or twice per term is enough. Never stuff keywords.
- Never add hidden text, white text or notes to AI screeners. Systems expose them, and recruiters reject them.

### What to cut

The resume stays short by leaving things out. Cut:

- duties with no result, such as "attended stand-ups" or "took part in sprint planning" (if the ad asks for Agile, cover it once in Skills);
- tools and topics the ad doesn't care about, unless they show a key strength;
- a bullet that proves the same point as another;
- soft-skill labels ("team player", "strong communicator"). Show them with a bullet instead;
- long technology lists under each job: name the key tools inside the bullets;
- interests and volunteering, unless the ad values them (for example community roles);
- referees' names and details (the last line covers them).

### Length and layout

- Two A4 pages at most: about 700 to 950 words and about 18 to 26 bullets in all. One page is fine for a short career.
- Use only headings, short paragraphs, "-" bullets and bold labels. No tables, columns, images, icons, emoji or code blocks.
- Leave a blank line between blocks. Without it, Markdown joins the lines into one paragraph.
- Bold only the labels (Skills rows, client roles and earlier roles). The headings are bold already.
- Write web addresses as plain text, for example "linkedin.com/in/name".

### Words and style

- Plain words. Australian spelling: organise, optimise, prioritise, colour, behaviour, centre, analyse, licence (the noun), program. Keep product names as their makers spell them.
- Spelling and grammar must be perfect. Typos cost interviews.
- Avoid these empty or AI-sounding words: passionate, results-driven, dynamic, proven track record, team player, hard-working, detail-oriented, self-starter, innovative, cutting-edge, world-class, seamless, synergy, spearheaded, leveraged, utilised, delve, showcasing, underscore, pivotal, crucial, testament, landscape, foster, elevate, empower. Also "responsible for", "worked on" and "duties included". Replace each with a specific fact.
- No em dashes (—). Use an en dash (–) only in date ranges.

## Step 3: check it against the ad (in your thinking, before you reply)

Keep each check to one line. Fix anything that fails. Then reply with the resume only.

1. **Must-haves:** each one marked strong or partial appears in the ad's words, in at least one bullet (or the summary). If it's a skill, it's in Skills too.
2. **Nice-to-haves:** each one I can prove appears at least once.
3. **No evidence:** items marked none aren't claimed or hinted at. (The cover letter deals with gaps.)
4. **Relevance:** each bullet backs up a must-have, a duty, or a top strength for this ad. Cut the rest.
5. **Top of page 1:** the summary and skills show the ad's job title words and its three biggest must-haves.
6. **Facts:** every title, employer, date, number and tool comes from my profile, with its label kept. Nothing from "Don't claim".
7. **Length:** two pages at most, within the word and bullet limits.
8. **Form:** the headings and order above; month and year on every role my profile gives them for; bullets start with varied verbs; no "I"; none of the avoided words; no em dashes; no tables; Australian spelling.
